# Scientific Computing {#scientific-computing}

#### 2001 - 2014 · UC Berkeley

::: {.chapter-intro}
Two projects from Berkeley's research labs became the dominant tools for how science and data engineering get done. One started as an afternoon of procrastination. One started because a classmate needed to win a competition. Both are now foundational infrastructure for AI.
:::

---

## Jupyter: The Procrastination That Runs Science

**The project:** IPython / Project Jupyter
**Campus:** UC Berkeley (BIDS)
**Period:** 2001 (IPython, begun at the University of Colorado Boulder [@ipython2026history]), 2014 (Project Jupyter)
**Key figures:** Fernando Pérez (creator; UC OSPO Network co-PI), Carol Willing (core developer, ACM Award; not UC-affiliated), Stéfan van der Walt (scikit-image)

::: {.origin-story}
*Section in preparation.*
:::

### Carol Willing and the Steering Council

Carol Willing is a core Jupyter developer, three-term Python Steering Council member, and Python Core Developer. She shared the 2017 ACM Software System Award for Jupyter's global influence - one of computing's most prestigious recognitions for software that has had lasting impact on the field. Willing was not based at a UC campus. Her role shows how a project that grew at Berkeley drew core contributors from elsewhere.

### What it became

Jupyter notebooks [@kluyver2016jupyter] are the dominant interface for interactive scientific computing worldwide. They run in data science courses, AI research labs, public health agencies, and science classrooms. JupyterHub scales the single-user notebook to institutional deployments serving thousands. Binder makes any notebook instantly reproducible and shareable. The format has become a de facto standard for communicating computational science.

## Apache Spark: From AMPLab to Apache

**The project:** Apache Spark
**Campus:** UC Berkeley AMPLab
**Period:** 2009
**Key figures:** Matei Zaharia, Holden Karau (PMC member, committer; not UC-affiliated)

::: {.origin-story}
*Section in preparation.*
:::

### Holden Karau and the core team

Holden Karau is a member of the Apache Spark Project Management Committee and a core committer who scaled Spark's Python and Core engines. She is the co-author of the definitive O'Reilly books *Learning Spark* and *High Performance Spark*, which trained a generation of Spark engineers. Karau was not at UC; her Spark work was done in industry, which is part of how a Berkeley project became an industry standard.

### What it became

Apache Spark [@zaharia2012spark] is the dominant framework for large-scale data processing. It powers data pipelines at virtually every major technology company and research institution. Databricks, founded by members of the Spark team, builds its business on it. The Apache Software Foundation stewards the open-source project; no single company can pull it away.
